title: Work-precision diagram: which solver is cheapest for a target accuracy?
summary: The fair way to compare numerical solvers: plot the cost (function evaluations) against the error actually achieved, on log-log axes. The cheapest solver for a given accuracy is the lowest curve at that error.

media.alt: Log-log plot of cost against achieved error for four solvers; error runs from 1e-3 on the left to 1e-10 on the right; four lines with markers, a high-order solver being cheapest at small errors; tolerance labels on one series.
media.caption: Reference render of class F5.9 (design-system gallery). The data are synthetic and exist only to demonstrate the form.

source.note: Plot class from the design system's plot taxonomy; synthetic demonstration data.

read_the_figure.question: Which solver is cheapest for a target accuracy?
read_the_figure.axes: x: achieved error, logarithmic and reversed so that accuracy improves to the right (1e-3 to 1e-10). y: cost in function evaluations, logarithmic (about 70 to 3e5).
look_at: At the accuracy you need, which curve is lowest?
Do any curves cross? Where, and what does that say about the best solver for loose and for tight tolerance?
What is the slope of each line? On these axes the slope relates to the order.
Are the points labelled by tolerance, so achieved error can be compared with requested error?
as_drawn: Four solvers: A (order 2), B (order 4), C (order 8) and D (implicit, order 3), each with eight points for tolerances from 1e-3 to 1e-10 (the x positions are the achieved errors).
B (blue squares) is cheapest at loose accuracy; the B and C lines cross near an error of about 2e-5, and C (amber triangles) is cheapest below that. A and D are the most expensive.
Tolerance labels are printed on solver B's points only, so the gap between requested tolerance and achieved error can be read for one series.
The x axis is reversed (lower error to the right); the label says lower is better, with an arrow.
read_the_figure.proves: The plot shows which solver is cheapest for a stated accuracy on the stated problem. Different problems, different cost measures (time rather than evaluations) or stiff cases can change the ranking, so the conclusion is conditional.
if_wrong: Lines that cross: there is no single best solver, which is the point of the plot; state the crossover.
Achieved error far from requested tolerance: the solver's error control is unreliable; compare at achieved, not requested, error.
A cost measure that ignores the Jacobian solves of an implicit method: the implicit solver is unfairly flattered.
must_check: log-log axes: cost and error both change by many decades, and the order of the method shows up as a slope only on log-log axes.
tolerance labels: they link the requested tolerance to the achieved error and cost, and show whether the solver meets its promise.

terms.meaning: A plot of the work (cost) needed to reach each accuracy, one curve per method.
A machine-independent count such as function evaluations; run time is an alternative but depends on the hardware.
The actual error of the run against a reference solution, as opposed to the tolerance that was requested.
The error the solver was asked to reach; adaptive solvers use it to choose steps.
The exponent in the error law e = C h^p. Cost scales as error to the power -1/p, so a higher order gives a flatter line.

remember: For a method of order p, cost scales as error to the power -1/p.
On log-log axes the slope of cost against error is -1/p: flatter means higher order.
Compare at achieved error, not at requested tolerance.
Cost counts function evaluations; check that implicit methods include Jacobian work.
The cheapest method depends on the target accuracy.

understand.title: Marks and encodings
understand.text: Each marker is one run at one tolerance; its horizontal position is the achieved error and its vertical position the cost. Each solver has its own colour, marker shape and line style. The reversed x axis puts more accurate runs to the right so that a line rising to the right reads as more work for more accuracy.

understand.title: Why this form answers the question
understand.text: Plain language: what you want is the cheapest way to get a given accuracy. This plot puts cost on one axis and accuracy on the other, so the answer is the lowest line at the accuracy you need. Higher-order methods give flatter lines: they cost a bit more at loose accuracy but much less as the target tightens, which is why curves cross.

understand.title: How it misleads
understand.text: The ranking applies only to the test problem. Function evaluations are not time: an implicit method does linear algebra on top of function evaluations that the count may ignore. A solver whose error control overshoots its tolerance will appear cheaper or dearer than it is if the plot uses the requested instead of the achieved error. Round-off will eventually flatten every curve to a vertical wall at small error, which this synthetic render does not show.

understand.title: Alternatives
understand.text: A table of cost at three target errors is easier for a decision. For one method, the error-against-step-size plot (F5.1) shows the order. For several problems, a performance profile (the fraction of problems solved within a factor of the best cost) removes the dependence on a single example.

understand.title: A variant to create
understand.text: Add a vertical dotted line at your required error, label the crossovers, add a hatched region at the round-off wall and plot a second panel with run time instead of function evaluations.

steps.title: Cost against error for order p
steps.note: On log-log axes this is a straight line of slope -1/p; the constant gamma maps tolerance to achieved error.

steps.title: Error reduction cost
steps.note: For orders 2, 3, 4 and 8 this is 10, 4.6, 3.2 and 1.8: cutting the error by 100 costs ten times more for A but under twice as much for C.

steps.title: Crossover of two solvers
steps.note: For the render's B and C this gives an error of about 2e-5; below it the order-8 solver is cheaper.

worked.title: Reading the cheapest solver from the reference render
worked.problem: (1) Which solver is cheapest at an achieved error of 1e-3 and at 1e-6, and about what are the costs? (2) What does A's slope say about its order? (3) How much more does it cost, for each solver, to reduce the error by a factor of 100?

solution.text: (1) At 1e-3 the lowest line is B, at about 70 evaluations (C needs about 120, A about 160); at 1e-6 the lowest is C at about 280 (B needs about 410, A about 5000, D about 11000).
(2) A's cost rises from about 1e2 to 3e5 over about 7 decades of error, so the slope on log-log axes is 0.5 in magnitude.

worked.answer: B at 1e-3 (about 70 evaluations) and C at 1e-6 (about 280); A's slope is -0.5 so it is second order; the order-8 solver pays only 1.8 times more for a hundred times less error.

analyze.q: Why do the B and C curves cross, and what would you advise for an engineer who needs 1e-3 versus one who needs 1e-9?
Solver D is implicit and sits above all the others. For which kind of problem might it overtake them?
Why is it more honest to use the achieved error than the requested tolerance on the x axis?
analyze.hint: Look at the tolerance labels on B.

evaluate.q: The plot shows C is cheapest at 1e-9. Does that justify using C for all your problems?
evaluate.hint: Smoothness, stiffness, cost measure, other problems.

create: Redraw the plot with run time on the y axis and compare the ranking with the function-evaluation version.
Add the round-off floor as a vertical wall and show one solver hitting it.

checks.q: What does a flatter line mean on this plot?
checks.answer: A higher order: the cost grows only slowly as the error requirement tightens.

checks.q: A solver of order 4 costs 400 evaluations at error 1e-4. Estimate the cost at 1e-6.
checks.answer: Cost rises by 100^(1/4) = 3.16, so about 1260 evaluations.

checks.q: Two curves cross at 1e-5. Which should you choose for a tolerance of 1e-3 and which for 1e-8?
checks.hint: Compare slopes: flatter wins at small error.
checks.answer: At 1e-3 the steeper (lower-order, cheaper-per-step) solver; at 1e-8 the flatter (higher-order) one, since its cost grows more slowly as accuracy tightens.
